newsitem.title: MALTA: MIDEAST MAY INTRUDE ON EUROPE-MEDITERRANEAN TALKS.
newsitem.headline: MIDEAST MAY INTRUDE ON EUROPE-MEDITERRANEAN TALKS.

text.p: Keeping a wary eye on the Middle East, European Union and Arab countries meet in Malta on Tuesday along with Israel and old foes Greece and Turkey to try to cement an EU-Mediterranean regional partnership.

EU council president Hans van Mierlo says the Arabs have agreed to leave Middle East problems aside at the two days of talks on advancing the 27-member EU-Mediterranean Partnership created in Barcelona in 1995.

But Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy will be at the same meeting for the first time since unrest broke out last month over Israel's building of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
The 15-member EU wants the talks to lay the groundwork for a Charter of Peace and Stability, bolster a regional free trade zone and increase cultural and social contacts.
"The charter is the most difficult task facing us," one EU official told Reuters, adding that economics and trade were mostly bilateral affairs and more easily handled.
Algeria, whose foreign minister Ahmed Attaf is spokesman for the Arab group, sees the problem differently:
"The EU priority is based on the political and security field to the detriment of the economic field", while the Arabs see economics as central to regional stability.
He also questions the European view of "security".

"When we wanted to introduce...the terrorism file in terms of organised cooperation, that brought resistance....," he said, referring to Algeria's longstanding objection to EU countries sheltering its Moslem rebel foes.
The EU's partners also object to its refusal to include Libya in the partnership, a view shared by host country Malta, which says Tripoli should be "part of the security structure".
Suspicions linger too that Europe, with 18 million jobless, wants to use any charter to curb immigration and push its ideas on democracy and human rights.
One Arab official commented: "The essential point for the countries of the south is that it (partnership) must not be seen just as a security problem...

"We understand that for Europe the problem involves illegal immigration, drug trafficking and the setting up of Islamic or other regimes that threaten Europe's security. We know this exists but it is only because there is an economic problem."
Europe's exclusion of farm products from plans for a free trade zone by the year 2010 in accords, like those signed with Tunisia, Morocco and Israel, is also questioned.
The southern countries are opening up to tough European industrial competition while Europe protects the agriculture of member countries like Spain, Portugal and Greece.
For the Middle East countries that hoped for the "dividend" of peace, economics and stability are inextricably linked.
"Lebanon's position is that there will be no involvement in any regional projects if the peace process is stumbling....," said its Foreign Ministry secretary-general Zafer al-Hassan.

While Arab countries want a higher EU profile in the Middle East, Israel insists Malta "cannot be a substitute for the existing framework of Israel-Arab negotiations or a forum for repeated condemnation of Israel...."

Palestinian cabinet secretary Ahmad Abdel-Rahman said: "We will be looking for development, political and economic support...Europe must have an effective role...not only as an observer but to be at the table with the other partners."

Trying to ease fears from Mediterranean countries that its economic interests lay only in eastern Europe, the EU promised more than $6.3 billion in grants, soft loans and development projects between 1995 and 1999.
Much of this has been accepted by Mediterranean countries for projects ranging from desert cultivation to establishing pro-democracy groups.

The EU has set aside $11.2 million this year to supplement the $12.6 million it has already spent on projects promoting human rights in the region. Five percent of this is dedicated to promoting harmony between Israelis and Palestinians.
